# Syncyard — agent skill

Syncyard is the one door between agents and the operator's own machines.
Programs do not dispatch GitHub Actions workflows directly, and they
never poll runs on their own. They submit job requests to the
**gatekeeper** (`gatekeeper/gk.py`, also reachable as `gh syncyard …`
when the gh extension is installed), which dispatches within the
shared API budget, assigns lanes, watches every run in one batched
sweep, and records verdicts. If you are an agent with work for the
operator's machines, work through the gatekeeper.

This skill tracks Syncyard version 0.2.0.

## The security invariant

Runners are reachable only via `workflow_dispatch` from the gatekeeper; no workflow may bind self-hosted labels to `pull_request`, `pull_request_target`, or issue events; the door repository is private; the backchannel repository is private.

Everything below is shaped by that invariant. Never propose, write,
or merge a workflow that weakens it. CI runs on GitHub-hosted
runners only. Never commit a token or credential anywhere.
Registration tokens are fetched at setup time and used once.
Runners register to the door repository only, never
organization-wide.

## Commands

```bash
GK="python3 gatekeeper/gk.py"     # or: gh syncyard

# Submit a Windows PowerShell job
$GK submit --program <your-program> --workflow run.yml \
    --lane <quick|normal|long|gpu> --script <script.ps1> \
    --cwd '<windows cwd>' [--expected-min N] --key <unique-key>

# Submit a WSL2 / Linux / macOS bash job
$GK submit --program <your-program> --workflow wsl.yml \
    --lane <lane> --script <script.sh> --cwd '<cwd>' \
    [--expected-min N] --key <unique-key>

# Return one file from the machine as an artifact (no script; path only)
$GK submit --program <your-program> --workflow grab.yml \
    --lane quick --grab-path '<path on the machine>' --key <unique-key>

# Register a run dispatched outside the gatekeeper (watch only)
$GK adopt --run-id <id> --program <your-program> --workflow <wf> \
    --lane <lane> --key <unique-key>

# The board: every tracked job, its state, flags, and verdict
# markers, plus queued/running counts and an ISSUES section
$GK status

# Hold ALL program dispatch (the watch pass keeps running;
# already-dispatched jobs are untouched — the gatekeeper
# never cancels). Maintenance jobs (--maintenance) still dispatch.
$GK pause --reason "operator working on the machines"
$GK resume

# The hard halt: sweeps no-op entirely until started again.
$GK stop --reason "fleet maintenance"
$GK start

# Push notifications instead of polling: register once with
# --notify-chat <endpoint> on submit/adopt; the coordinator
# delivers start / completion / escalation pushes from the outbox.
$GK outbox
```

- Every job carries a **unique `--key`**. Submitting a key that is
  already active is refused and prints the existing job — that
  refusal is the duplicate-dispatch pre-check working. Never work
  around it by changing the key for the same work; check
  `gk status` instead.
- `--expected-min` matters for `long` and `gpu` jobs: health
  watermarks are judged against the declared expectation before
  lane defaults.
- `gk cancel <id-or-key>` is local bookkeeping for jobs that were
  never dispatched. It never cancels a GitHub run. No command in
  this system cancels a running job — see escalation below.
- The status board's **ISSUES** section is the operator's problem
  list: watermark breaches and escalations, failed or pending log
  harvests, a dispatch stuck needing a human, and completions with
  no marker verdict. Read it before concluding the fleet is healthy.
- Every gatekeeper state write is write-verify-retry (spec 001
  FR-012/FR-013): a record's file is only ever replaced by renaming
  a fully verified temp file over it, so a failed save can never
  destroy the standing record. Never treat a 0-byte state file as
  real, and never trust an unverified write.

## Periodic status-check duty (spec 009 FR-005)

**Every agent that uses Syncyard checks Syncyard status before
submitting work for the machines, and at least once per hour during
an active campaign on them.** Use `gk status` when the gatekeeper
is reachable; otherwise use the failsafe backchannel's read-only
status (`backchannel/bc.py heartbeat` / `bc.py status`). A stale
backchannel heartbeat (older than 5 minutes), a down supervisor
tray, or a down runner is **reported to the operator's Syncyard
coordination point** — never worked around, never routed around
silently, and never a reason to improvise an alternate route to
the machines.

## Lane routing

Every dispatch declares a lane. **No lane declared = not dispatched.**

| Lane | Expected duration | Use for |
|---|---|---|
| `quick` | under ~2 min | probes, status checks, small transfers |
| `normal` | ~2–30 min | builds, installs, packaging |
| `long` | over ~30 min, or unknown | batch stages, scoring runs, renders |
| `gpu` | any duration | any job that needs a GPU |

- **GPU overrides duration.** A 30-second GPU probe goes to `gpu`,
  never to `quick`. A long GPU render goes to `gpu`, never to `long`.
- **Unknown duration goes to `long`.**
- A job that overruns its lane's norm twice gets re-laned in its
  program's briefs (quick → normal, normal → long), and the overrun
  is reported.
- Detached background processes on a machine are not Actions jobs
  and do not take a lane; the status checks *about* them are
  `quick` jobs.
- Jobs expected to exceed 60 minutes are announced to the
  coordination point before dispatch, with their expected duration.
- GitHub's job execution limit is exactly 360 minutes; longer work
  is designed as chunked/resume-safe stages or a detached,
  checkpointed process the gatekeeper probes — never one long run.

## Marker verdicts

**A job's verdict comes from the marker lines it prints in its own
log — never from the GitHub Actions success color alone.** Platform
run status has been observed frozen at "queued" long after a job's
log held its complete result; the log is the record.

- Write every job script to print unambiguous marker lines with its
  results, for example `PROBE_DONE gpus=2 free_gb=212` or
  `BUILD_VERDICT: PASS`. Markers are lines that begin with an
  `ALL_CAPS_` token; the gatekeeper harvests exactly those.
- Read verdicts from `gk status` or from the job record the
  gatekeeper keeps, not from the Actions web UI.
- A run that "failed" according to a client printout but whose
  markers say otherwise gets cross-checked against the actual job
  log before anyone believes either.

## API discipline

The GitHub REST quota (5,000 calls/hour) is one account-wide bucket
shared by every program. The gatekeeper exists so the fleet spends
it once, centrally. Your obligations:

- **Never poll a run yourself.** The gatekeeper's sweep (every
  5 minutes) is the only watcher. If you truly must look, one
  batched `gh run list` covering all your runs, no faster than
  every 3–5 minutes — never a per-run loop, never `gh run watch`
  left running (its default interval is ~3 seconds).
- **Before any burst of API calls** (more than ~10), run
  `gh api rate_limit` — the endpoint is free. Core remaining
  **below 1,000**: stand down to minimum cadence and say so in
  your report. **Below 500**: completion-critical calls only, at
  most one per 5 minutes.
- **A 403 rate-limit response is a hard stop** for that scope.
  Stop, do not retry through it, report the rate-limit snapshot
  and reset time. Resume only after the reset *and* a fresh
  headroom check.
- Dispatch only needed jobs. No speculative duplicates; cancel your
  own superseded queued work through your coordinator.

## Watermarks and escalation etiquette

Each lane has warning watermarks for queue wait and execution time
(defined in the gatekeeper's config). The gatekeeper records
breaches; it **never cancels anything**. Your conduct when a breach
involves your job:

- **Queued breach = starvation.** Your job is the victim, not the
  problem. Never cancel it. The lane ahead of it is what gets
  escalated.
- **Executing breach = stall suspect.** Check step progression in
  the record: a job whose step advanced is slow, not stalled — say
  so and stand down to second-warning watch.
- If machine state is needed to tell slow from wedged, that takes a
  quick-lane probe job (process list, GPU state, disk, venue log
  tail). A probe that never returns reclassifies the event as a
  machine-level problem.
- Escalate to the coordination point at the second warning, with
  the evidence: run id, lane, dispatch time, watermark breached,
  signals observed, probe result.
- **Cancellation authority is narrow:** only your own program's
  coordinator, after a recorded check — or the owner. Never another
  program's watcher, never automatically, never for a queued
  breach.

## Windowless supervision

The runners run under a supervisor (the Syncyard Tray on Windows;
systemd units on Linux/WSL targets), never as hand-started console
windows:

- Runners stay in the owner's interactive session on purpose: jobs
  need the owner's WSL distro, GPU, audio, and bench devices, which
  a Windows service in session 0 cannot reliably reach. Do not
  register the runners as services.
- Runner directories live under the owner's profile — never in a
  drive root.
- A job script that starts a program starts it hidden or headless
  and cleans it up when the job ends; a visible window or a
  lingering process after a job is a defect in that script.

## Board (hardware) scenario jobs

Jobs that touch physical hardware (development boards on a bench
station) follow an extra discipline on top of everything above:

- They run **one at a time under a claim**: the job registers its
  claim before its first hardware step and releases it with actual
  times when done. Claims are never silently stacked.
- The first step is always a **reachability and identity proof** in
  the execution context that can actually reach the hardware.
  Failure aborts before any claimed act.
- Safety gates that protect the hardware are **hard steps inside
  the job**: a failed gate aborts before any step that depends on
  it.
- Physical acts are **exactly-once**: jobs are idempotent or check
  a consumed-marker before repeating an act.
- Steps only a human can do (power cycles, cable moves) are
  terminal states: the job stops and reports "human step required".
  No retry loops against physical hardware.
- The job **harvests before it exits**: all logs and captures are
  copied off the device before the job ends; results left only on
  the device mean the job failed.

## Failsafe backchannel (spec 009)

Syncyard has a failsafe backchannel for the case where Syncyard
itself — the runners, the tray, or gatekeeper dispatch — is down
or blocked. It is deliberately narrow:

- **Channel**: `syncyard-dev` in the **private** backchannel
  repository — `channels/syncyard-dev/cmd.json`, `out.json`, and
  `heartbeat.json`.
- **Owner**: the operator's Syncyard coordination point only. It is
  the sole poster to the channel. No other chat or agent may post
  to it.
- **No program job traffic, ever.** The backchannel carries only
  Syncyard development and recovery work (for example: restart the
  runner supervisor in the owner's session, read its log, restart
  a runner lane, run read-only network diagnostics). Programs keep
  using the gatekeeper in all circumstances.
- **Desktop side**: `backchannel/agent.sh` runs as a systemd user
  service under the owner's WSL/Linux user, independent of the
  runners, tray, and gatekeeper. It syncs over git (no REST quota),
  executes only a command whose id is new and whose sha256 matches
  its body, writes `out.json` matched by id, and heartbeats every
  poll cycle (~60 s). A `channels/syncyard-dev/STOP` file halts
  execution while the heartbeat continues. It never writes
  gatekeeper queue records.
- **Client**: `backchannel/bc.py heartbeat|status|send|wait`
  (Python stdlib only). `send` refuses to overwrite an
  unacknowledged pending command unless `--force`, stamps a unique
  id + the sha256 of the body, and verifies by reading `cmd.json`
  back.
- **Your part**: read-only. Use `bc.py heartbeat` / `status` for
  the FR-005 status check when the gatekeeper is unreachable, and
  report a stale heartbeat (>5 min) or a down tray/runner to the
  coordination point. Recovery procedures live in
  `backchannel/RUNBOOK.md`.

## Break-glass

The operator keeps a separate, frozen emergency admin path outside
Syncyard, for the case where the Actions route itself is broken.
It carries **no job traffic, ever** — not for convenience, not for
speed, not because the queue is long. If you believe the emergency
path is genuinely needed (the gatekeeper cannot dispatch and the
runners cannot be reached), stop, say exactly that, and let the
owner decide. Do not improvise alternate routes to the machines.

## Keeping this skill current (standing rule)

**This skill is updated in the same change as any change to
Syncyard behavior, commands, lanes, workflows, or operations.** A
change that leaves the skill stale is incomplete. All editions of
this skill are generated from one shared source
(`skills/_source/contract.md`) so their content cannot drift; the
repository's CI verifies every edition against that source, the
release VERSION, and the security invariant above.
